pages.title: Lagavulin distillery - Wikipedia
pages.description: Encyclopedia entry on Lagavulin distillery on Islay, its owners and its whisky.
pages.text:
Lagavulin distillery is an Islay single malt Scotch whisky distillery in the village of Lagavulin, on the south of the island of Islay, Scotland. Owner: Diageo. Founded: 1816. Capacity: 1,400,000 L.

History
The distillery of Lagavulin officially dates from 1816, when John Johnston and Archibald Campbell Brooks built two distilleries on the site. One of them became Lagavulin and took over the other; which one is not exactly known. Records show illicit distilling in at least ten illegal distilleries on the site as far back as 1742.

John Johnston ran the distillery until 1835, when it was valued at £1,103 9s 8d. Alexander Graham then took it over and made his son Walter Graham the distiller. Walter ran it until 1848, when he moved to Laphroaig. John Crawford Graham later went into partnership with James Logan Mackie, who was left in charge from 1856. Peter Mackie joined his uncle's firm in 1878, and in the mid-1880s they set up Mackie & Co. Peter Mackie leased Laphroaig, and legal battles followed. He became sole partner in 1889. In 1895 the two businesses joined as Mackie & Co (Distillers) and began to blend White Horse with Lagavulin whisky.

In the early 1920s Iain Ramsay sold the distillery to Peter Mackie for £16,000. In 1923 the firm was acquired by Buchanan Dewar Ltd. The company joined Distillers Company in 1925. Distillers Company was acquired by Guinness in 1986, and Guinness merged with Grand Metropolitan to form Diageo in 1997.

The 16-year-old won four double gold medals in a row at the San Francisco World Spirits Competition, 2005 to 2008.

pages.title: Lagavulin | Scotch Whisky
pages.description: Whiskypedia entry on Lagavulin with its history, timeline and owners.
pages.text:
Lagavulin. Distillery & brand. Region: Islay. Status: Working. Lagavulin 16 Year Old joined the Classic Malts in 1989.

History
On Islay's south (Kildalton) coast, between Ardbeg and Laphroaig, legal distilling at Lagavulin was started in 1816 by John Johnston. A second distillery on the site was first bought by the same family in 1825, and its production was absorbed into Lagavulin in 1837. It came to wider notice in 1862 when blender John Logan Mackie bought the distillery. His nephew Peter J. Mackie later took over production and created White Horse in 1890. In 1908, annoyed at losing the Laphroaig agency, Mackie built a replica distillery at Lagavulin called Malt Mill. It ran until 1962. The distillery floor maltings shut in 1974.

Timeline
1816 Lagavulin is founded by John Johnstone
1836 Johnstone dies; Alexander Graham buys the distillery
1837 The two distilleries are merged and operated as Lagavulin
1862 Lagavulin moves into the hands of James Logan Mackie & Co
1889 James Logan Mackie dies; his nephew Peter Mackie takes control
1908 Mackie builds a second distillery on the site, Malt Mill
1927 White Horse Distillers becomes part of DCL
1941 The distillery is closed for the rest of WWII
1951 A destructive fire breaks out
1962 Malt Mill is closed
1974 Lagavulin's floor maltings are decommissioned
1988 Lagavulin 16 Year Old is selected as one of the six Classic Malts

Owners
Diageo 1997 - present; United Distillers 1986 - 1997; Distillers Company Limited 1927 - 1986; White Horse Distillers 1924 - 1927; Mackie & Co 1867 - 1924; John Johnstone 1816 - 1837

pages.title: History - Lagavulin Distillery
pages.description: Difford's Guide history of Lagavulin distillery on Islay's south-east coast.
pages.text:
Lagavulin Distillery. Status: Operational. Established: 1816. Owner: Diageo plc. Visitor Policy: Visitors welcome throughout the year.

Pronounced 'lagga-Voo-lin', from the Gaelic Laggan Mhouillin, 'the mill in the valley'. The distillery sits on the water's edge in a small bay on Islay's south-eastern coast, near the ruins of Dunyveg Castle.

Illicit distilling was recorded on the site as early as 1742, but the distillery dates from 1816, when John Johnston built Kildalton Distillery at Lagavulin. The following year Archibald Campbell built a second distillery named Lagavulin beside it, which Johnston also acquired in 1825. The two distilleries merged to become Lagavulin in 1837 under the ownership of the Graham brothers and James Logan Mackie. Peter Mackie worked for his uncle at the distillery before setting up his own company, Mackie & Co. Distillers Limited, in 1883. He then inherited Lagavulin in 1890.

A second distillery, Malt Mill, opened 1908. An explosion and fire in 1952 led to a rebuild that brought the mash tuns fully under cover. Malt Mill closed in 1962 and its stills moved to Lagavulin's still-house. All four stills were converted to steam heating in 1969.

After Peter Mackie's death in 1924 the company took the name White Horse Distillers Limited. Three years later it became part of the Distillers Company Limited (DCL), now part of Diageo.

Barley for Lagavulin is malted at nearby Port Ellen. Fermentation runs up to 75 hours.

Lagavulin 8 Year Old 200th Anniversary Bottling: released in March 2016 to celebrate the distillery's 200th anniversary.

pages.title: Lagavulin Distillery :: Islay Info
pages.description: Islay visitor guide to Lagavulin distillery, with a short history and opening times.
pages.text:
Lagavulin Distillery is one of the three Kildalton distilleries in the south of Islay, in a small bay between Ardbeg and Laphroaig. It officially dates from 1816, though records show illicit distilling on the site as far back as 1742. By 1837 the two original distilleries, built by John Johnston and Archibald Campbell, had been combined and were occupied by Donald Johnston. In the 19th century there were several legal battles with neighbouring Laphroaig over Lagavulin making a replica whisky. In 1962 the still house was rebuilt with the pear-shaped stills of the Malt Mill Distillery, and in 1996 a new mashtun and automated controls were fitted. For most of the 1980s the distillery worked just two days a week; production rose in the 1990s. It is owned by Diageo plc.

The distillery produces about 1.4 million litres of alcohol per year, with water from Lochan Sholum. Malted barley has come from Port Ellen Maltings since 1974, after floor malting ended.

The visitor centre dates back to 1998, in the buildings that were once the maltings and kiln of Malt Mill Distillery.

Opening 2026-27: Monday-Sunday 10am-5pm until the end of October, with fewer days and shorter hours from November to February. Tours include the new Warehouse No3 cask draw experience. Updated 8 April, 2026.

expected.notes: opened 1816: all four pages (Wikipedia: officially dates from 1816, and Founded: 1816; ScotchWhisky.com: legal distilling started in 1816, and the 1816 timeline entry; Difford's Guide: Established: 1816 and dates from 1816; Islay Info: officially dates from 1816).

notes: Conflicts: (1) The Mackie purchase. ScotchWhisky.com gives 1862 in its history and timeline but its owners list starts Mackie & Co in 1867; Wikipedia says James Logan Mackie was in charge from 1856. A source that gives two values supports neither, so an acquired event for Mackie is optional and must not be dated by guesswork. The first name is John Logan Mackie in the ScotchWhisky.com history and James Logan Mackie in its timeline and on Wikipedia. (2) The move to DCL: Wikipedia says the company joined Distillers Company in 1925; ScotchWhisky.com says 1927 (timeline and owners list); Difford's Guide says "three years later" than 1924, which states no year. Both stated years come from reference pages, so neither clearly wins; an acquired event for DCL is optional, and if kept it should cite each source with its own statedValue. (3) The fire: 1951 on ScotchWhisky.com, 1952 on Difford's Guide. (4) Peter Mackie's control: sole partner 1889 (Wikipedia, ScotchWhisky.com timeline) against inherited in 1890 (Difford's Guide); Mackie & Co set up in the mid-1880s (Wikipedia) against 1883 (Difford's Guide). (5) Founders: Wikipedia has John Johnston and Archibald Campbell Brooks building two distilleries in 1816; Difford's Guide has Campbell building the second the following year. (6) Johnston left in 1835 (Wikipedia) or died in 1836 (ScotchWhisky.com). Optional events: Malt Mill 1908 to 1962, the 1941 wartime closure, the 1969 change to steam heating, the 1996 new mashtun, and acquired 1986 (Guinness) and 1997 (Diageo). Traps: the 1742 illicit stills are not the founding; the Classic Malts selection (1988 in the timeline, 1989 in the intro), the 16-year-old's medals, the 8 Year Old 200th Anniversary Bottling and the 2026-27 opening hours are bottle, award or visitor details; the 1998 visitor centre is a visitor detail. The 1.4 million litres of alcohol a year (Islay Info) is a valid LPA capacity site fact; Wikipedia's 1,400,000 L does not say LPA. No official page is included: the Malts.com page and canmore.org.uk returned no text. Peated stores the owner Diageo and the Malts.com page as website. Page texts are reviewed paraphrases of the cited pages, not copies. Generic events are allowed but never required, so these are not expected: generic 1837, the two distilleries on the site merged as Lagavulin, and generic 1974, floor maltings ended.
